name: Narration Visual Character Alignment
source_tutorial: project lesson: Bleach women recap correction, 2026-06-23
use_when: A recap, commentary, explainer, or documentary narration names a person, character, place, object, product, UI element, proof point, or scene event.
The edit uses source footage while the original source audio is muted or replaced by narration.
A character-specific section could accidentally inherit a shot from the previous or next character.
The viewer may judge timing by rounded playback timestamps such as 0:42 rather than the exact EDL boundary.
avoid_when: The visual mismatch is intentional irony, foreshadowing, or contrast and the user has approved it.
The narration is intentionally abstract and does not require literal visual correspondence.

timeline_pattern.early_handoff_rule: For named entities, the supporting visual should arrive slightly before the viewer-facing timestamp. Do not rely on an exact sub-second EDL boundary if the user or platform player will show the rounded second.
timeline_pattern.spot_check_window_rule: When checking a reported timestamp, inspect at least 0.5s before through 1.0s after the complaint window, plus the full named-entity section.
timeline_pattern.source_identity_rule: Verify the source range by looking at frames, not by assuming that a nearby source section contains the right character or subject.
timeline_pattern.rendered_output_rule: The final proof must come from the rendered preview or promoted final, not only from the EDL or source contact sheet.

motion.rule: Reframes, zooms, effects, or speed changes must preserve the named character, object, or proof point throughout the narrated reference.
motion.avoid: Using a stronger-looking shot that belongs to a different character or topic during a named narration beat.

sound.rule: When original source audio is muted and narration drives meaning, visual timing follows the narration track, not the source scene order.
sound.avoid: Letting music or source rhythm justify a visual mismatch with the spoken name.

captions.rule: If captions are present, caption timing and visual timing should agree on the same named entity unless the mismatch is approved.
captions.avoid: Captioning one character or topic while the picture still shows another.

color.rule: Grade continuity is secondary to subject correctness. A visually pretty shot fails if it shows the wrong entity.

implementation.ffmpeg: After rendering preview/final, extract timestamped contact sheets around each named handoff, for example with fps=1, drawtext timestamp labels, and tile. Review the cells that correspond to the actual viewer-facing seconds.
implementation.remotion: Represent narration cues with entity labels and require each visual segment to declare the matching entity, expected output window, and reviewed frame samples.
implementation.blender: Use only for planned illustrative transitions; rendered frames still need entity-match review against the narration cue.
implementation.capcut_equivalent: Place markers at each spoken name, start the matching shot a fraction early when needed, and watch the exported file at those timestamps.
implementation.premiere_equivalent: Use sequence markers for spoken names and export frame/contact sheets around each handoff before final delivery.

common_mistakes: Trusting that an EDL boundary like 42.765s is enough when the viewer sees the player at 0:42.
Checking only the source range or the timeline and not the rendered output.
Using a visually exciting shot from the wrong character because it feels close in mood or color.
Fixing one section while accidentally leaving a one-second carryover from the previous section.
Looking only at the exact complaint timestamp instead of the surrounding playback second.
qc: For every named character, person, place, object, product, UI element, or proof point, is the matching visual already visible at the viewer-facing timestamp?
Does the visual handoff happen early enough that rounded player times do not show the previous subject?
Have source ranges been verified visually before assignment?
Have timestamped contact sheets been generated from the rendered preview or final around each sensitive handoff?
If the user reports a timestamp, was at least 0.5s before through 1.0s after that window inspected?
Does the promoted final file, not just the preview, pass the same spot check?
